blocks.text: The results of mechanical tests are usually expressed in terms of stress and strain, which are defined in terms of applied force and deformation.

blocks.title: Stress
blocks.text: Stress is the force applied per unit area to produce any change in the shape, volume or length of a body: stress (sigma) = force (F) / area (A) ... (5.1). The SI unit of stress is the newton per square metre (N m^-2), given the name pascal (Pa). When a stress changes length it is called tensile stress, when it changes volume it is volume stress, and when it changes shape it is shear stress.

blocks.title: Strain
blocks.text: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it. For deformation in one dimension, strain is the fractional change in length: if delta L is the change in length and L the original length (Fig. 5.3a), strain (epsilon) = change in length (delta L) / original length (L) ... (5.2). Being a ratio of lengths, strain is dimensionless and has no units. Strain due to tensile stress is tensile strain, and strain produced by compressive stress is compressive strain. When the applied stress changes the volume, the change in volume per unit volume is the volumetric strain (Fig. 5.3b): volumetric strain = delta V / V ... (5.3). If y is the distance between two opposite faces of a rigid body subjected to shear stress and one face slides through delta x (Fig. 5.3c), the shear strain is gamma = delta x / y = tan theta ... (5.4); for small theta measured in radians tan theta is about theta, so gamma = theta ... (5.5).

blocks.title: Young's modulus
blocks.text: The stress applied per unit strain is called Young's modulus: Y = tensile stress / tensile strain = (F/A) / (delta L / L) ... (5.6). It has the same unit as stress, N m^-2 or Pa. Although named after the 19th-century British scientist Thomas Young, the concept was developed in 1727 by Leonhard Euler (For Your Information). There are various methods to determine the Young's modulus of a wire; one is Searle's method.
